title: The configuration management process
blurb: Order the five configuration management activities and recognise each one in a scenario.
question: On a payroll system upgrade, the team must decide how documents will be named, label every item, stop unapproved edits, report which versions are current and check everything before go-live. Which configuration management activity is each of these, and in what order do they come?

teach.body: A typical configuration management process has five activities: planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification audit. Plan how you will manage the items; identify and label them; control changes to them; keep account of their status; then audit that items and records really match. Scenario: Orbit, a council payroll system upgrade, whose specifications, designs, test scripts and user guide all need managing.

steps.label: Planning
steps.sub: How items will be identified, controlled, recorded, audited; by whom

steps.label: Identification
steps.sub: Choose and uniquely label the items; set the baseline

steps.label: Status accounting
steps.sub: Record and report status, version and history

steps.label: Verification audit
steps.sub: Items match requirements; records match reality

teach.caption: Control is where configuration management links to change control.
Pirates plan the raid, identify the treasure, control who touches it, keep an account of it, then verify the haul.

teach.body: Planning comes first. Orbit's configuration management plan sets the naming convention, the tool that stores the items, who may change what, how status is reported and when audits happen. Identification then applies it: the team decides which items need control, gives each a unique reference and version, and records the agreed set as the baseline.

teach.caption: Every item gets a unique reference and version, using the convention set during planning.

teach.body: Control means only authorised changes are made. At Orbit, a developer checks out PAY-DES-004, and a new version is only checked back in when change control has approved the change. Status accounting records and reports where every item stands: its current version, whether it is draft or approved, and its full change history. It answers 'which version is current?'

head: Item
Version

teach.caption: Anyone can see which version to use, and how each item got there.

teach.body: Before Orbit goes live, the quality lead runs a verification audit. Do the delivered items match their requirements? Do the records match reality: is the user guide in use really v1.0, as the report says? Was every change authorised? Any gap is corrected before handover. Audits can also be held at other key points, not just the end.

teach.caption: Control acts on changes, status accounting keeps the record, verification audit checks the record is true.

teach.text: 'Evaluation', 'Registration' and 'Justification' are NOT configuration management activities. And don't mix up identification (giving items unique references) with status accounting (recording their current state and history).

items: Five activities in order: planning, identification, control, status accounting, verification audit.
Planning: how items will be identified, controlled, recorded and audited, and by whom.
Identification: uniquely label each item and set the baseline. Control: only authorised changes are made.
Status accounting records current status, version and history. Verification audit checks items and records match reality.

summary: You can now list the five configuration management activities in order and explain what each one does. You can also recognise each activity in a project scenario and avoid the distractor activities the exam offers.

A.q: Which is the first activity in a typical configuration management process?
A.why: Planning comes first: it sets out how items will be identified, controlled, recorded and audited, and by whom.

whyNot.0: Identification is second; it applies the conventions decided in planning.
whyNot.1: Status accounting is fourth, once items exist and are under control.
whyNot.3: Control is third, after the items have been identified.

A.q: Which configuration management activity gives each item a unique reference and establishes the baseline?
A.why: Identification selects the configuration items, labels each one uniquely and sets the baseline.

whyNot.1: Verification audit checks items and records; it does not create references.
whyNot.2: Status accounting records the state of items that have already been identified.
whyNot.3: Planning decides the naming convention; identification applies it to each item.

A.q: Which activity records and reports the current version and change history of each configuration item?
A.why: Status accounting records and reports the current status, version and change history of every item.

whyNot.0: Control makes sure only authorised changes are made; it does not report status.
whyNot.1: Planning decides how status will be reported, but does not do the reporting.
whyNot.2: Verification audit checks the records are accurate; it does not keep them.

B.q: Which list shows the configuration management activities in the correct order?
options: Planning, control, identification, status accounting, verification audit
Planning, identification, control, status accounting, verification audit
Identification, planning, control, verification audit, status accounting
Planning, identification, status accounting, control, verification audit
B.why: The order is planning, identification, control, status accounting, verification audit.

whyNot.0: Items must be identified before changes to them can be controlled.
whyNot.2: Planning comes before identification, and status accounting before the audit.
whyNot.3: Control comes before status accounting: changes are controlled, then recorded.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT an activity in a typical configuration management process?
B.why: Evaluating changes belongs to change control. The five configuration management activities are planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification audit.

whyNot.0: Status accounting is the fourth configuration management activity.
whyNot.1: Verification audit is the fifth configuration management activity.
whyNot.2: Control is the third configuration management activity.

B.q: At Orbit, a developer must check out the interface design, and a new version can only be checked back in once the change is approved. Which activity is this?
B.why: Control makes sure only authorised changes are made and versions are managed.

whyNot.1: Identification labelled the design; it does not govern later changes.
whyNot.2: Planning set the check-out rule, but applying it day to day is control.
whyNot.3: Status accounting records the new version afterwards; it does not gate the change.

C.q: Before go-live, Orbit's quality lead compares each delivered item with its requirements and with the configuration records. Which activity is this?
C.why: Verification audit checks that items meet their requirements and that the records match reality.

whyNot.0: Status accounting keeps the records; the audit checks that they are true.
whyNot.2: Identification labels items at the start; it does not check them against requirements.
whyNot.3: Control gates changes; it does not compare delivered items with the records.

C.q: Orbit's PM wants a report showing which items are approved, which are still draft and which have changes pending. Which activity provides it?
C.why: Status accounting records and reports the current status of every item.

whyNot.0: Planning decides what the report will contain, but does not produce it.
whyNot.1: Identification gives items their references; it does not track their status over time.
whyNot.3: Verification audit checks the accuracy of records rather than producing routine status reports.

C.q: Which TWO activities take place before configuration control? 1. Planning 2. Status accounting 3. Identification 4. Verification audit
C.why: Planning (1) and identification (3) come before control; status accounting and verification audit come after it.

whyNot.1: Both status accounting (2) and verification audit (4) come after control.
whyNot.2: Verification audit (4) is the last activity, after control.

reteach.title: Think of writing a family cookbook
reteach.question: Twenty relatives are sending recipes for a printed family cookbook. How do you make sure the right version of every recipe ends up in print?

blocks.h: Five steps to a cookbook with no mistakes
blocks.body: First you agree the rules: how recipes are numbered, where they are kept and who may edit them (planning). Each recipe gets a number and version, like R-012 v1 (identification). Only the editor can approve changes, so Uncle Tom cannot quietly add more chilli (control). A tracker shows each recipe's latest version and status (status accounting). Before printing, you check the proof against the tracker (verification audit).

blocks.text: The tracker (status accounting) and the proof check (verification audit) are different jobs: one keeps the record, the other proves the record matches what is actually going to print.

explain.body: Decide, before anything else, how configuration items will be identified, controlled, recorded and audited, and who is responsible. Usually written up as a configuration management plan.

test.q: What is decided during configuration management planning?
options: How items will be identified, controlled and audited
Which change requests the sponsor will approve
Which risks will be transferred to a supplier
How the budget will be split across all work packages
test.why: Planning sets out how configuration items will be identified, controlled, recorded and audited, and by whom.

whyNot.1: Approving change requests is a change control decision.
whyNot.2: Transferring risks is a risk response.
whyNot.3: Splitting the budget across work packages is cost planning.

explain.body: Choose which items need control, give each a unique reference and version, and record the agreed set as the baseline. You cannot control something you have not identified.

test.q: Which of these is an example of configuration identification?
options: Approving a request to change a test script
Labelling the test scripts PAY-TST-012 v1.0
Checking the test scripts match the records
Reporting how many scripts are still draft
test.why: Giving an item a unique reference and version is identification.

whyNot.0: Approving a change request is change control.
whyNot.2: Checking items against records is verification audit.

explain.body: Once items are identified, only authorised changes are made to them, and versions are controlled. This is where configuration management meets change control: no approval, no new version.

explain.h: Can a new version be checked in?

test.q: What is the main aim of configuration control?
options: Every item is given a unique reference
The records are checked against reality
Only authorised changes are made to items
The current status of every item is reported
test.why: Configuration control makes sure only authorised changes are made, with versions controlled.

whyNot.0: Giving items unique references is identification.
whyNot.1: Checking records against reality is verification audit.
whyNot.3: Reporting current status is status accounting.

explain.body: Record and report the current status, version and change history of every item. It is how anyone can find out which version to use and how it got there.

test.q: Complete the statement: status accounting is the recording and reporting of…
options: each change request's cost and benefit
each team member's hours on the project
each risk's probability and impact score
each item's current status and history
test.why: Status accounting records and reports every configuration item's current status, version and change history.

whyNot.0: Costs and benefits of a change are assessed in change control's evaluation stages.
whyNot.1: Hours worked are tracked through resource and cost management.
whyNot.2: Probability and impact are recorded in risk management.

explain.body: Check that the items meet their requirements and that the records match reality. It confirms the configuration is what everyone believes it to be, and that only authorised changes were made.

explain.caption: A mismatch like the user guide must be investigated and corrected.

test.q: A verification audit finds the user guide in use is v2.2, but the records say v2.1. What has the audit done?
options: Approved the user guide for release
Found records that do not match reality
Given the user guide a new identifier
Planned how the guide will be controlled
test.why: A verification audit checks that records match reality; here it has found a mismatch to investigate.

whyNot.0: An audit checks; it does not approve items for release.
whyNot.3: Deciding how items will be controlled is planning.
